My name is Kya Vulgamott, and I am a senior in the undergraduate Public Health program at San Diego State University (SDSU). SDSU has a prominent Reserve Officers’ Training Corps (ROTC) program due to its proximity to Camp Pendleton, and I’ve had the privilege of forming close friendships with several ROTC members. Over the past five years, I’ve witnessed a significant increase in participation in the ROTC program, and I feel compelled to share my concern about the Department of Veterans Affairs’ proposed reinstatement of abortion and abortion counseling exclusions in VA and CHAMPVA medical benefits.
I would like to specifically comment on the language found on page 36416 of the Federal Register, where the term “elective abortion” is used and where it states that abortion will be excluded except when “a physician certifies that the life of the mother would be endangered if the fetus were carried to term.” The rule also asserts, “No State law prohibits treatment for ectopic pregnancies or miscarriages to save the life of a mother.”This language is misleading in the current legal climate. For example, in Ohio, women can be charged with fetal manslaughter in certain miscarriage cases, introducing fear and legal uncertainty around accessing care. Additionally, the rule only considers physical threats to a pregnant person's life and fails to consider mental health crises, which are a critical part of overall health.
The U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs confirms that Veterans are at a significantly higher risk of experiencing mental health crises, including depression, PTSD, and substance use disorders, than the civilian population. These factors can influence the viability or outcome of a pregnancy and contribute to increased rates of non-viable pregnancies or the inability to parent a child safely. Mental health is not a secondary concern; it is essential to comprehensive, adequate health care.
By eliminating access to abortion counseling and services—even in complex mental health circumstances—this proposal neglects the emotional well-being of veterans and their families. It also removes a layer of emotional support that may be vital for people undergoing pregnancy termination, especially in cases of trauma, sexual assault, or service-related psychological injuries.
I recommend that the VA Redefine “life-threatening” illnesses to include conditions that present serious mental health risks, including PTSD, major depression, and suicidal ideation. Further, reallocating funding from military weapons development toward military medical training programs would reduce costs of care and improve internal medical capacity. By providing access to medical training, veterans would be almost guaranteed post-service employment for medical personnel trained during military service. Access to these trained professionals would strengthen the veteran care pipeline and encourage quality care within VA facilities, potentially even on a volunteer basis by those who are no longer active duty. Continuing the ideal of volunteer services, the VA could establish support groups as an alternative to formal therapy to provide emotional support for veterans navigating reproductive health decisions.
The current proposed rule reinstating abortion exclusions under VA and CHAMPVA programs overlooks critical aspects of veterans’ mental health, emotional well-being, and the complex realities of reproductive health care. By addressing only physical danger and excluding emotional and psychological factors, the rule fails to serve the holistic needs of those who have served our nation.
I respectfully urge the Department of Veterans Affairs to reconsider its definition of “needed medical services” to include mental health-related pregnancy risks, invest in medical training within the armed forces, and create emotionally supportive networks for veterans navigating reproductive care.
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on this critical issue.
